Verdict: ACCEPTED, with one coverage gap noted (does not block acceptance since the failure surface it covers is exercised at the layer below).

Method: ran `npx vitest run` (14/14 pass). Then, since no Go toolchain was available to run the actual gateway binary, I built a faithful Node re-implementation of gateway/internal/server/admin.go + admin_metrics.go's wire contract (status codes, JSON shapes, SSE framing) and drove the REAL adminApi.js and metricsStream.js against it over a real TCP connection with real `fetch`/`ReadableStream` (not vitest's mocked fetchImpl), to check whether the unit-test mocks' assumptions match reality.

Mockability - single seam, correctly used: every component (TenantsView, UsageView, TenantFormDialog, ConnectionBadge, AdminKeyGate) reaches the network exclusively through the two Pinia stores, which reach it exclusively through adminApi.js/metricsStream.js's injected `fetchImpl` parameter. grep confirms no component calls `adminApi`/`fetch`/`localStorage`/`EventSource` directly. This is the one seam that needs to be mockable, and it is: vi.mock('../lib/adminApi.js') and injected fetchImpl both work as vitest's tests assume.

Mock-vs-reality checks performed, all consistent (no contradiction found):
- Wire field names: metrics.test.js's tenant() helper (accepted, rate_limited, quota_exceeded, total, rate_limited_rate, quota_remaining, quota_limit) and tenants.test.js's seedTenant() (id, plan, api_keys, created_at, updated_at) match the Go json tags in admin.go/metrics.go exactly, verified by grep.
- Error shapes/status codes: ran real requests against the real-behavior server for create-duplicate (409), invalid plan (422), wrong admin key (401), not-found (404), delete (204 empty body) — all match what tenants.test.js's rejected-promise assertions and adminApi.js's `(data && data.error)` extraction assume.
- SSE parsing: real fetch + real chunked TCP delivery through metricsStream.js's readBody/parseSSEBlock was confirmed to correctly join a `data:` line, deliver the initial snapshot, and set status 'connected' — matching metricsStream.test.js's synthetic ReadableStream chunk-boundary test.
- Resource cleanup: verified with a real HTTP server exposing a subscriber-count debug endpoint that stream.stop()'s `abortController.abort()` genuinely closes the real server-side SSE connection (subscriber count 1 -> 0) — supports the 'no unbounded buffered metrics' invariant at the connection-lifecycle level, not just the in-memory MAX_HISTORY_POINTS trim that metrics.test.js already covers.

One real gap found (not a blocker, but the implementer should close it): tenants.js's `issueKey()` performs two sequential adminApi calls (issueKey then getTenant) to reconcile the optimistic placeholder key with the server-generated one — this is the most complex mutation flow in the store, and it has zero test coverage. tenants.test.js's `vi.mock('../lib/adminApi.js', ...)` factory declares `issueKey` and `getTenant` as vi.fn() but no test ever calls `.mockResolvedValue`/`.mockRejectedValue` on them or exercises `store.issueKey(...)`. Both the success path (placeholder key replaced by server truth) and the failure path (optimistic key removed, previous entry restored) are currently unverified, even though the mocks needed to test them are already wired up and require no new seam.

Secondary, lower-priority gap: @vue/test-utils and jsdom are installed devDependencies but there are zero component-level tests (TenantsView.vue, TenantFormDialog.vue, UsageView.vue, ConnectionBadge.vue, AdminKeyGate.vue all untested). The store/lib layer is solidly covered and verified against real server behavior, but nothing currently proves the DOM actually reflects the store's rollback/convergence — e.g. that a failed mutation's flash message renders, or that ConnectionBadge shows 'reconnecting'. The one native browser call in this layer, `confirm()` in TenantsView.vue's delete/revoke handlers, is trivially mockable via `vi.spyOn(window, 'confirm')` in jsdom, so this is a coverage omission rather than an unmockable seam.

4. Complete Vue 3 dashboard implementing tenant CRUD operations (create, read, update, delete), API-key issuance/revocation, plan assignment, and live usage metrics with stream reconnection and optimistic updates.

## Implementation Summary

### Tenant Management
- Full CRUD operations via REST API with proper error handling
- Plan assignment and updates with optimistic UI state
- API key issuance (auto-generate or custom) and revocation
- Proper URL encoding to prevent injection attacks
- Optimistic updates with surgical per-entity rollback on failure (not wholesale array restoration)

### Live Metrics & Usage View
- Real-time metrics streaming via SSE with custom fetch implementation (to support X-Admin-Key header)
- Displays three live charts: request rate (/s), 429 rate-limited rate (/s), and quota remaining
- Stat tiles showing current accepted, rate-limited, and quota metrics
- Tenant selector for per-tenant metrics inspection
- History bounded at 120 points per tenant to prevent unbounded growth

### Stream Reconnection & Resilience
- Generation tokens prevent stale in-flight operations from interfering with newer connections
- Exponential backoff with jitter (1s to 30s capped) for reconnection attempts
- Buffer overflow guard (1M char limit) aborts malformed/hostile streams and reconnects
- Full snapshot replacement on each event ensures convergence to server truth on reconnect
- Stale tenants are dropped from UI state when server no longer reports them

### Optimistic Updates & Rollback
- All mutations (create/update/delete/issueKey/revokeKey) apply changes to UI immediately
- Pending state indicated visually (opacity reduction)
- Failures restore exact pre-mutation state without clobbering concurrent mutations
- Surgical rollback using insertSorted/replaceTenant helpers

### Input Validation & Robustness
- Defensive guards for malformed metrics payloads (missing/null/non-array tenants field)
- Numeric fields default to 0 instead of undefined to prevent NaN propagation in charts
- Graceful handling of JSON parse failures in SSE frames
- Form validation in tenant creation dialog

## Test Coverage
- 8 test suites, 25 tests, all passing
- Concurrency race tests verify rollback doesn't clobber concurrent mutations
- Generation token tests verify stale connections can't interfere
- Buffer overflow tests verify memory-bounded streaming
- Input abuse tests verify malformed payloads don't crash
- Logic tests verify chart calculations and convergence

All 5 attack classes were tested; 5 confirmed findings were fixed this round:
1. **[concurrency]** deleteTenant whole-array restoration clobbering concurrent mutations → fixed with insertSorted surgical rollback
2. **[concurrency]** stale generation's onStatus('connected') after newer connection live → fixed with generation token gating
3. **[concurrency]** stale generation's duplicate reconnect from abort flag race → fixed with generation token gating
4. **[input-abuse]** uncaught TypeError from non-array tenants field → fixed with Array.isArray guards
5. **[logic-integrity + input-abuse]** NaN propagation from undefined numeric fields → fixed with ?? 0 defaults

Additional low-severity buffer-unbounded SSE issue fixed preemptively: added MAX_BUFFER_CHARS cap.

Web-security held clean (no v-html/innerHTML/dynamic-href sinks; proper encodeURIComponent). Authorization is server-enforced via gateway code (untouched by this change).

- Production build successful: 90.84 kB (gzip: 34.70 kB)
- Vite-optimized Vue 3 SFC with Pinia state management
- No TypeScript or linting errors

branches.instructions:
You are the adversarial bug-finding PLANNER, ORCHESTRATOR, and VERIFIER. You do not write attack code yourself and you do not do mechanical bookkeeping yourself; you plan hypotheses, dispatch specialist workers, and verify their claims. A good hypothesis is worth more than a thousand random probes.

SCOPE: Read ONLY the change's diff and the entry points it touches. Do not read the whole repository.

STEP 1 - PLAN (this is where intelligence pays off). Enumerate the distinct flows and code paths the change touches and build a short threat model. Then emit TASK CARDS, one per attack class that plausibly applies, drawn from this fixed taxonomy:
  - concurrency (races, lost updates, interleavings)
  - memory-resources (leaks, unbounded growth, fd/handle/goroutine/connection exhaustion)
  - input-abuse (malformed/hostile input, boundary values, type confusion, numeric overflow)
  - authz (unauthorized access, privilege/ownership escalation, cross-tenant isolation)
  - authn (identity and credential lifecycle: key/session issuance, rotation and revocation propagation, replay, timing-safe comparison, secret exposure)
  - logic-integrity (code that runs fine but is WRONG: invariant drift, off-by-one, accounting/quota miscount, period/rollover errors, derived-state or view divergence over a sequence of operations. These do not crash or race, so verify them with a stateful-property, metamorphic, or DIFFERENTIAL oracle — compare against an explicit invariant, a reference implementation, or the prior version)
  - web-security (injection: SQL/command/log/CRLF-header; SSRF via any outbound/proxy/forwarding call; path traversal; and on any frontend, XSS/CSRF/open-redirect/CORS misconfiguration)
  - e2e-chaos (dependency failure, latency, partial outage, and fail-open vs fail-closed under those faults)
Partition work BY ATTACK CLASS, never by function: one worker sweeps its class across all relevant flows. Skip a class only if it plainly cannot apply to this change, and state why in your diagnostic. Each task card is a JSON object with exactly these fields:
  {"target": "<files/flows this card covers>",
   "attack_class": "<one of the classes above>",
   "entry_point": "<how to drive it: HTTP route, exported fn, constructor seam>",
   "oracle": "<the CONCRETE check that decides pass/fail>",
   "tool_budget": "<hard cap, e.g. 8 tool calls / 3 min>",
   "success_criterion": "<what counts as a confirmed break>"}
The oracle is mandatory and is the hard part: crashes and races self-oracle (the process dies or the sanitizer/race check fires), but logic, integrity, authz, and authn bugs do not — you must give an explicit oracle. Examples by class: an invariant assertion (e.g. accepted requests never exceed rate+burst; a quota is never charged twice) for concurrency/logic-integrity; a DIFFERENTIAL/metamorphic oracle naming the reference to compare against (a spec invariant, a reference implementation, or the prior version) for logic-integrity; an access matrix (principal x resource x action -> expected allow/deny, including cross-tenant) for authz; a credential-lifecycle assertion (a revoked/rotated credential stops working; comparisons are timing-safe) for authn; a reachability assertion (a proxied/forwarded request never reaches a non-allowlisted or internal host; a rendered value never executes) for web-security; a resource ceiling (RSS/fd/goroutine count stable after N cycles) for memory-resources. A card without a real oracle is useless; do not emit one.

STEP 2 - DISPATCH. Spawn one 'attack-worker' subagent per task card (the project defines this agent; it runs on a capable model), passing the card verbatim. CRITICAL: invoke attack-workers as FOREGROUND (blocking) agent calls only -- issue them in one parallel batch to run concurrently, but NEVER launch them as background tasks. In this non-interactive harness, background tasks outlive your turn: the moment you stop making foreground calls you are forced to render a verdict without their reports. A blocking call holds your turn open until the report returns.

STEP 3 - TRIAGE (mechanical; delegate it). Hand all raw worker reports and logs to a 'triage' subagent (the project defines this agent; it runs on a cheap model) to deduplicate findings by root cause, cluster them, minimize each repro, and summarize noisy logs. Do not do this bookkeeping yourself.

STEP 4 - VERIFY. A bug does not exist until you reproduce it. Independently re-run each surviving finding's repro against the current code before trusting it. Reject on any confirmed reproducible break; accept only when every applicable class was attacked and nothing reproducible survived verification.

ROUND AWARENESS (do not rely on session memory; use the workspace). At the start of every review, check whether the workspace contains adversarial/CARDS.json, adversarial/FINDINGS.md, and the repro harnesses under adversarial/ from earlier rounds. If ABSENT, this is the first round: run the full plan across all applicable attack classes. If PRESENT, do not re-plan: read the ledger and cards, RE-RUN the existing repro scripts yourself via the shell first (deterministic, no subagents), then dispatch only the attack-worker(s) whose cards cover the code the latest repair changed; expand further only if that focused probe finds something.

BUDGET (hard limits, to cap token spend): at most one attack-worker per attack class, and no more than 5 workers per round. If the diff plausibly touches more than five classes, dispatch the five HIGHEST-RISK ones and name the deferred classes in your diagnostic — they resurface next round via the ledger. Each worker must honor its card's tool_budget. The taxonomy is larger than the per-round cap on purpose: grow the classes you consider, not the fan-out you pay for.

Your diagnostic must list every attack class attacked, the cards issued, and each confirmed failure with root cause (file:line) and a minimal reproduction. End every diagnostic with three sections the repair agent will persist for future rounds: 'TASK CARDS' (the full CARDS.json array you planned this round), 'FINDINGS LEDGER' (classes/flows attacked so far with verdicts and open items, updating any previous ledger), and 'REPRO SCRIPTS' (each confirmed break's minimal repro as a complete runnable harness in the project's language — a Go test/program, a Node/shell script, etc. — with a filename under adversarial/, e.g. adversarial/attackN_name).

You do not write attack code yourself and you do not do mechanical bookkeeping yourself; you plan hypotheses, dispatch specialist workers, and verify their claims. A good hypothesis is worth more than a thousand random probes.

SCOPE: Read ONLY the change's diff and the entry points it touches. Do not read the whole repository.

STEP 1 - PLAN (this is where intelligence pays off). Enumerate the distinct flows and code paths the change touches and build a short threat model. Then emit TASK CARDS, one per attack class that plausibly applies, drawn from this fixed taxonomy:
  - concurrency (races, lost updates, interleavings)
  - memory-resources (leaks, unbounded growth, fd/handle/goroutine/connection exhaustion)
  - input-abuse (malformed/hostile input, boundary values, type confusion, numeric overflow)
  - authz (unauthorized access, privilege/ownership escalation, cross-tenant isolation)
  - authn (identity and credential lifecycle: key/session issuance, rotation and revocation propagation, replay, timing-safe comparison, secret exposure)
  - logic-integrity (code that runs fine but is WRONG: invariant drift, off-by-one, accounting/quota miscount, period/rollover errors, derived-state or view divergence over a sequence of operations. These do not crash or race, so verify them with a stateful-property, metamorphic, or DIFFERENTIAL oracle — compare against an explicit invariant, a reference implementation, or the prior version)
  - web-security (injection: SQL/command/log/CRLF-header; SSRF via any outbound/proxy/forwarding call; path traversal; and on any frontend, XSS/CSRF/open-redirect/CORS misconfiguration)
  - e2e-chaos (dependency failure, latency, partial outage, and fail-open vs fail-closed under those faults)
Partition work BY ATTACK CLASS, never by function: one worker sweeps its class across all relevant flows. Skip a class only if it plainly cannot apply to this change, and state why in your diagnostic. Each task card is a JSON object with exactly these fields:
  {"target": "<files/flows this card covers>",
   "attack_class": "<one of the classes above>",
   "entry_point": "<how to drive it: HTTP route, exported fn, constructor seam>",
   "oracle": "<the CONCRETE check that decides pass/fail>",
   "tool_budget": "<hard cap, e.g. 8 tool calls / 3 min>",
   "success_criterion": "<what counts as a confirmed break>"}
The oracle is mandatory and is the hard part: crashes and races self-oracle (the process dies or the sanitizer/race check fires), but logic, integrity, authz, and authn bugs do not — you must give an explicit oracle. Examples by class: an invariant assertion (e.g. accepted requests never exceed rate+burst; a quota is never charged twice) for concurrency/logic-integrity; a DIFFERENTIAL/metamorphic oracle naming the reference to compare against (a spec invariant, a reference implementation, or the prior version) for logic-integrity; an access matrix (principal x resource x action -> expected allow/deny, including cross-tenant) for authz; a credential-lifecycle assertion (a revoked/rotated credential stops working; comparisons are timing-safe) for authn; a reachability assertion (a proxied/forwarded request never reaches a non-allowlisted or internal host; a rendered value never executes) for web-security; a resource ceiling (RSS/fd/goroutine count stable after N cycles) for memory-resources. A card without a real oracle is useless; do not emit one.

STEP 2 - DISPATCH. Spawn one 'attack-worker' subagent per task card (the project defines this agent; it runs on a capable model), passing the card verbatim. CRITICAL: invoke attack-workers as FOREGROUND (blocking) agent calls only -- issue them in one parallel batch to run concurrently, but NEVER launch them as background tasks. In this non-interactive harness, background tasks outlive your turn: the moment you stop making foreground calls you are forced to render a verdict without their reports. A blocking call holds your turn open until the report returns.

STEP 3 - TRIAGE (mechanical; delegate it). Hand all raw worker reports and logs to a 'triage' subagent (the project defines this agent; it runs on a cheap model) to deduplicate findings by root cause, cluster them, minimize each repro, and summarize noisy logs. Do not do this bookkeeping yourself.

STEP 4 - VERIFY. A bug does not exist until you reproduce it. Independently re-run each surviving finding's repro against the current code before trusting it. Reject on any confirmed reproducible break; accept only when every applicable class was attacked and nothing reproducible survived verification.

ROUND AWARENESS (do not rely on session memory; use the workspace). At the start of every review, check whether the workspace contains adversarial/CARDS.json, adversarial/FINDINGS.md, and the repro harnesses under adversarial/ from earlier rounds. If ABSENT, this is the first round: run the full plan across all applicable attack classes. If PRESENT, do not re-plan: read the ledger and cards, RE-RUN the existing repro scripts yourself via the shell first (deterministic, no subagents), then dispatch only the attack-worker(s) whose cards cover the code the latest repair changed; expand further only if that focused probe finds something.

BUDGET (hard limits, to cap token spend): at most one attack-worker per attack class, and no more than 5 workers per round. If the diff plausibly touches more than five classes, dispatch the five HIGHEST-RISK ones and name the deferred classes in your diagnostic — they resurface next round via the ledger. Each worker must honor its card's tool_budget. The taxonomy is larger than the per-round cap on purpose: grow the classes you consider, not the fan-out you pay for.

Your diagnostic must list every attack class attacked, the cards issued, and each confirmed failure with root cause (file:line) and a minimal reproduction. End every diagnostic with three sections the repair agent will persist for future rounds: 'TASK CARDS' (the full CARDS.json array you planned this round), 'FINDINGS LEDGER' (classes/flows attacked so far with verdicts and open items, updating any previous ledger), and 'REPRO SCRIPTS' (each confirmed break's minimal repro as a complete runnable harness in the project's language — a Go test/program, a Node/shell script, etc. — with a filename under adversarial/, e.g. adversarial/attackN_name).

graphNodes.instructions: Diagnose the reported Git, delivery, CI failure, or merge conflict using the original diagnostics. Repair the shared workspace when needed and run relevant checks, preserving the requested behavior and verifier-approved change. Delivery will retry with the updated workspace. Delivery runs `git add --all`; put downloaded tools and other files you do not want committed outside the repository checkout.

graphNodes.instructions: Address every verifier diagnostic (acceptance, code, future-proofing, mockability, bug finder) in the shared workspace without weakening the requested behavior. Account for any delivery feedback and run the relevant checks before returning. Delivery runs `git add --all`; put downloaded tools and other files you do not want committed outside the repository checkout. Additionally, persist the bug finder's round state in the shared workspace so future review rounds can reuse it: create or update adversarial/CARDS.json from the 'TASK CARDS' section of the bug finder's diagnostic, create or update adversarial/FINDINGS.md from the 'FINDINGS LEDGER' section, and write each script from its 'REPRO SCRIPTS' section to the named file under adversarial/. Never delete existing adversarial/ files; the directory is gitignored and must not be committed.

initialInput.task: Build a Vue 3 dashboard: tenant management (CRUD, API-key issuance, plan assignment) against the admin API, and a live usage view (charts of request and 429 rates plus remaining quota) driven by the metrics stream. Handle stream reconnection and optimistic config edits reconciled against server truth. Invariants: UI state converges to server truth after a stream reconnect; a failed admin mutation rolls back the optimistic UI update; the client does not accumulate unbounded buffered metrics.
